criterion_notes.c1: Discusses household and community rural water and sanitation service delivery and access in South Africa, including piped household connections, communal standpipes, and unmaintained rural infrastructure.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (yes under plain reading) because it discusses municipal governance, accountability, participatory structures (ward committees, Citizen's Voice, The Water Dialogues), and NGO/CBO institutional dynamics in water delivery, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (no under active reading) because it examines broad participatory governance, gender hierarchies in sector organisations, and a generic technicist project-delivery paradigm rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (passing secondary mentions of Free Basic Water standards, water charges, prepayment meters, and CBO commercialisation are illustrative background only). Note that plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the article also fails Criteria 3, 4, and 5 as a non-empirical Perspective essay.
criterion_notes.c3: Published under the journal's 'perspective' rubric, this article is a reflective commentary/narrative essay drawing broadly on 20 years of experience, secondary literature, and previously published reports (e.g., Galvin 2009, 2010a, 2010b; Water Dialogues DVD 2009). It reports no empirical study design, sampling, data-collection methods, or systematic synthesis protocol, and presents no primary empirical analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report empirical outcomes on household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion; rural coverage and standpipe statistics from secondary sources are cited as background motivation while the essay focuses on barriers to community/women's participation and sector paradigm change.
criterion_notes.c5: As a non-empirical Perspective essay without reported methods or primary sample, an identifiable empirical study design, study sample, rule-type exposure, and measured service-access outcome cannot be established.

evidence_quotes.quote: This Perspective draws together and reflects on primary research conducted by the author over the past decade regarding the barriers to ‘real’ participation of community members

It asserts one perspective and experience of organisations in order to highlight issues that typically remain unquestioned. It does not attempt to definitively attribute meaning or motivation to any organisation.

Stakeholders described the existing paradigm as characterised by a technicist approach in which infrastructure is provided, with little or no differentiation between local contexts, histories, or needs.

The impact of the paradigm is most severe in rural areas, where 70 per cent of South African women live below the monthly poverty line (R515 per person in 2008) and only 15 per cent of households have piped water/household connections (Casale and Posel, 2010).
The Water Dialogues achieved openness on the part of all stakeholders about problems in ensuring ‘real’ participation at the municipal and national levels in the sector.

raw_response.exposure: Technicist service delivery paradigm, organisational/gender power dynamics, and barriers to community participation in water governance (no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism empirically analysed)
raw_response.outcome: Barriers to and openings for women's and community participation and accountability in water governance (rural water access statistics cited only from secondary sources as background)
raw_response.population_and_sample: not reported (broad reflective discussion of rural women, communities, CBOs, NGOs, and municipalities in South Africa without an empirical study sample)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). Published in Agenda's 'perspective' section, Galvin (2011) is a reflective commentary and narrative overview essay drawing broadly on secondary literature and the author's previously published reports (e.g., The Water Dialogues synthesis report) without reporting an identifiable empirical study design, sample, data-collection methods, or primary empirical data analysis. In addition, while the essay would satisfy the plain broad governance wording of Criterion 2 (discussing participatory governance and institutional dynamics), it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (focusing on a generic technicist delivery paradigm, organisational gender hierarchies, and broad citizen participation rather than an analysed rule-type mechanism governing access) and focuses on participation processes rather than empirical service-access outcomes (Criterion 4). Because it fails Criterion 3 regardless of how Criterion 2 is read, both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
